stories.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, faster and cheaper, and it tops Artificial Analysis at 65
stories.why_read: This is the biggest model drop of the week and the HN thread is past 800 comments. If you pick models for agents or coding work, the new pricing and the deliberate capability caps both change the math.
body: Anthropic says Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model: Fable carries strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards so it can go to everyone, while Mythos is reserved for vetted orgs in its Cyber and Life Sciences Verification Programs. The release claims gains in coding, reasoning, and vision, output up to 30% faster than the 5.1 models, and a lower price of $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, with an optional fast mode at up to 2.5x speed for double the price. In prerelease testing Anthropic says the model helped finish otherwise-infeasible migrations, designed three working electronic devices, and formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours.

Artificial Analysis now ranks Fable 5.2 (max) first of 74 models on its Intelligence Index with a 65, while also flagging it as slow, verbose, and the most expensive per task. The debate on X is about what Anthropic left out: it says it deliberately held training in areas like accelerator kernel optimization and LLM architecture research to older Opus 5.5 levels, grouping them with cyber and bio risk, which open-source advocates read as a move to slow frontier AI research.

stories.headline: Tesla will end Cybertruck production in about eight months to focus Giga Texas on Cybercab
stories.why_read: This is the clearest sign yet that Tesla is betting the Austin factory on robotaxis. It's a local story for you, and it changes what Giga Texas builds.
body: Elon Musk said Tesla will shut down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory in roughly eight months so the plant can ramp Cybercabs instead, with many deposits set to be returned. His reasoning is that the truck's manufacturing complexity makes it the wrong use of the line, even though orders still outpace output.

The numbers behind the call are stark: around 56,000 Cybertrucks delivered over four years against an original plan of 250,000 a year, and recent changes already stopped new orders for one trim while raising prices on another. The Texas plant is aiming for more than 125,000 Cybercabs a year, and the open question in the replies is whether Tesla could have run both vehicles side by side.

stories.headline: Grok 4.8 finishes pre-training on a stack rewritten in C and C++, with a soft rollout to Grok Bot users this week
stories.why_read: The model you use every day through Grok Bot is about to change, and the team threw out JAX and SGLang to get there. That's an unusual systems bet worth understanding.
body: Musk says Grok 4.8 has wrapped pre-training and moved into reinforcement learning after the SpaceXAI team replaced JAX and SGLang with custom C code plus some C++. The rewrite cost development time but is meant to pay off in long-term speed and performance, and cleaning up the training data also improved results.

A soft rollout to Grok Bot users is slated for later this week to test real-world use, and Musk says this version won't resemble Grok 4.7. At SpaceX the model is already at work spotting debris in rocket parts (see the borescope story below).

stories.headline: Nvidia unveils GR00T 2, an open world-action model for robots, at CoRL in Austin
stories.why_read: The Conference on Robot Learning is in your town this week, and Nvidia used it to show one model handling grippers, hands, and humanoids. If physical AI is the next platform, this is the reference stack.
body: GR00T 2 predicts both video frames and robot movements, and was trained on more than 400,000 hours of human video plus robot data. Nvidia says it succeeded on 40 unseen tasks with no prior demos and reached 95% success after quick fine-tunes. A Turbo version runs on Jetson Thor for on-robot use, and code is due in December.

Partners launched alongside it: Skild AI open-sourced Steel, a physics solver built with Nvidia inside the open-source Newton engine that it says delivers up to 13 times PhysX throughput on mixed tasks, and Nvidia shipped Isaac Lab 3.0 updates. CoRL runs November 9 to 12 at venues including the JW Marriott Austin.

stories.headline: Amazon swaps Claude Sonnet 4.6 for a small decision model on ticket labeling and cuts cost 98%
stories.why_read: This is a concrete, measured case for not using a frontier LLM where a classifier will do. If you run agents at enterprise scale, the architecture pattern is directly reusable.
body: Two Amazon engineers describe replacing Sonnet 4.6, which had been labeling tickets across one of the world's largest internal ticketing systems into 20 categories, with Strands Decider. A decision model doesn't generate text: it takes some state and a set of options and returns a probability for each plus a confidence score, which maps neatly onto ticket in, label out.

They tested the original 2B model, then switched to an E4B Gemma 4 build that did clearly better, tuned the confidence threshold, and saw it beat production Sonnet on a separate ticket set at 98% less cost. It runs on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances with one A10G each, using about 19 GiB and roughly 640 ms per request, and they say the change saves millions of dollars in tokens a year.

stories.headline: SpaceX says Grok catches rocket debris on borescope video at 99.9% accuracy, versus 94% for human inspectors
stories.why_read: It's a rare real-world number for AI in aerospace quality control, and it ties Grok directly to launch safety. One miss in 1,000 instead of one in 17 is a big deal at Starship cadence.
body: SpaceX VP Kiko Dontchev said at last week's UP Summit in Florida that Grok analyzes borescope videos of rocket tubes for foreign object debris, catching it 99.9% of the time compared with 94% for human inspectors. That moves the miss rate from about one in 17 to one in 1,000.
Dontchev said tools like this have cut engineering tasks from hours to seconds, calling it the biggest gain he has seen in 16 years at the company, as SpaceX ramps its launch rate.

stories.headline: More than 40% of GitHub pull requests now start with an AI agent, up from 17% six months ago
stories.why_read: You reposted this one, and it's the number behind the whole 'software factory' debate. The question is shifting from who writes code to who reviews and secures it.
body: 1Password's developer account highlighted that over 40% of pull requests on GitHub now begin with an AI agent, up from 17% just six months earlier, and argued the interesting part isn't just who writes the code.

The stat is fueling a wider argument on X: Matt Pocock calls today's engineers 'factory engineers' who design pipelines for agents, while skeptics such as Mario Zechner and J.F. Puget warn that review skills still matter because agents can ship flawed code or slow down simple tasks.

stories.headline: A breach at inference provider Fireworks AI exposed some Notion AI chat transcripts
stories.why_read: Third-party inference is now part of your supply chain. This is a clean case study in what a vendor breach looks like when you serve open-weight models through someone else.
body: Notion says fewer than 1% of workspaces may be affected after its vendor Fireworks AI reported that malicious actors may have accessed customer data. The exposed material was unattributable Notion AI chat transcripts used for its Insights feature, meaning no labels tying them to a user or workspace and no tool-call results.

Notion had used Fireworks for classification behind Insights and as a general inference provider for open-weight models. It cut all connections when it first heard of potential incidents, Fireworks confirmed the new dataset on November 8, Insights is disabled for now, and Notion no longer serves open-weight models through Fireworks.

stories.headline: A researcher documents consumer Gemini sending connected Drive files and emails to human reviewers
stories.why_read: If anyone in your family connects Gmail or Drive to consumer Gemini, this is worth five minutes. The finding is that lookups can happen without an explicit @Drive or @Gmail tag.
body: A GitHub write-up argues Google quietly reversed its 2023 promise that personal Gmail, Docs, and Drive content connected to Gemini 'is not seen by human reviewers', pointing to an updated Google help article and an October 16 edit to the original blog post that warns reviewers may see an email or file.

The author says testing shows ambient mentions of personal topics like trips or bills can trigger background Workspace lookups, and that what gets captured is probabilistic. A clarification notes this applies to personal @gmail.com accounts; Workspace business, enterprise, and education accounts are covered by separate terms that exclude human review by default.

stories.headline: DeepMind's AlphaProof Code formally verifies the actual code behind the Signal protocol
stories.why_read: Agents writing millions of lines of machine-checked proof against production crypto is a new bar for software assurance. Paired with today's CPython story, verification is having a moment.
body: Google DeepMind says researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the real implementation of the Signal protocol, which protects conversations in Signal and Google Messages. It calls this the first time a widely deployed protocol implementation has been formally verified at this depth by any method.

AlphaProof Code splits the work like a research team: humans and models translate security goals into formal specs, with experts reviewing each one, then agents running Gemini Carbon write the proofs, more than six million lines of Lean. The agents then flag about 1% of the codebase for a human second look, since Lean checks the rest automatically.

stories.headline: Agents copy CPython into 613,000 lines of Lean and turn up 418 bug reports
stories.why_read: This shows what agent-scale formal methods do to a codebase everyone runs. About 55 of the bugs can crash the interpreter or corrupt memory from ordinary Python.
body: David Andrews and Chao Zhang pointed Opus 5.5 at CPython and had it rewrite functions line by line in Lean. Each copy is tested against real Python on tens of thousands of inputs before any proof is attempted, and a function only counts once a second agent that didn't write it checks the work. So far 4,071 functions have passed, totaling 613,318 lines across 1,539 files with 18,898 theorems and lemmas.

Coverage is uneven: about 16% of CPython 3.15.2 overall, with grammar rules at 100% and the standard library at 9%. The motivation is that Python has no precise written definition beyond whatever CPython does, so a checked model of it is useful well beyond bug hunting.

stories.headline: Charlie Marsh had Codex build a CPython bytecode compiler in Rust that matches CPython byte for byte
stories.why_read: From your bookmarks. When the uv team says an agent-built compiler might ship, it's a strong data point for what coding agents can do on real infrastructure.
body: Astral's Charlie Marsh says Codex built `serc`, a CPython bytecode compiler written in Rust that emits byte-for-byte identical output on the top 10,000 PyPI packages while running 2 to 4 times faster than CPython's own implementation.
He calls it entirely an experiment, but says it may ship as an opt-in feature in uv.

stories.headline: Meta's Muse Ember aims to be the cheapest model for the work agents repeat all day
stories.why_read: Small, fast models are where agent costs actually live. Meta says this one beats Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna on intelligence per dollar.
body: Meta introduced Muse Ember as its smallest and most efficient model, built for tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. It claims Ember matches Haiku's best Artificial Analysis score at about a third of the cost and beats every GPT-6 Luna setting.
On Meta's own chart, Ember scores 35.8 at about $0.136 per task, versus 36.2 for Haiku 5.5 at its max setting for about $0.411. Meta notes Ember's costs are estimates at proposed pricing.

stories.headline: What Uber's 800-server MCP gateway teaches everyone else, plus MCP gets events
stories.why_read: You reposted both of these. Together they sketch where enterprise agent plumbing is heading: one identity-aware gateway, and agents that subscribe instead of poll.
body: Uber Engineering described an MCP Gateway hosting more than 800 MCP servers and over 5,000 tools. An AutoCrawler scans Uber's IDL registry and turns HTTP, gRPC, and TChannel APIs into tools that start disabled until the owning team enables them, and an Omni MCP proxy lets agents discover servers and tools incrementally instead of loading everything into context. Speakeasy's Sagar Batchu added that full API coverage is the wrong goal, non-technical staff are some of the heaviest MCP users, and gateways must attribute every call to a human, agent, or delegated identity.

Separately, Vercel's Guillermo Rauch said MCP was missing a way to tell an agent later that something happened, and that MCP Events fixes it. Vercel's MCP now publishes events such as deployment.succeeded and deployment.error with webhook notifications, so an agent no longer has to poll.

stories.headline: Langfuse launches an AI Gateway in public beta: change one base URL and every request becomes a trace
stories.why_read: From today's bookmarks. If you're thinking about cost tracking and governance across OpenAI and Anthropic, this is the low-effort version.
body: Langfuse says every company needs one way to use models, track costs, and govern access to AI. Its new gateway sits in front of OpenAI and Anthropic, and swapping a single base_URL turns each request into a Langfuse trace.
It's in public beta, and it lands in the same week as the Uber and Speakeasy gateway debate above.

stories.headline: Grok Bot outbound calls can now run up to 115 minutes, up from 85
stories.why_read: You reposted this. Thirty more minutes per call is exactly what insurance and pharmacy hold queues need.
body: Grok Bot's outbound phone calls can now last up to 115 minutes each, 30 minutes more than before. Daily limits are unchanged at 10 calls a day and up to 4 to the same number.
The pitch in the post is simple: long hold times with insurers or the pharmacy stop being a problem when the bot can wait them out.

stories.headline: CoreWeave's bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress spreads after the election
stories.why_read: The AI buildout runs on debt, and lenders are repricing it. Watch this if you care about who keeps getting GPUs next year.
body: CNBC reports CoreWeave's bond yield has climbed above 16%, and default protection costs have risen across AI-linked names: credit default swaps on Nvidia debt are up 76% in a month, Broadcom 49%, and Amazon 44%, though spreads stay far lower than CoreWeave's roughly 1,100 basis points. Jefferies' Christopher Wood put it bluntly: the arms race most plausibly ends when 'the credit card will be taken away.'

Markets are weighing delays under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia; Goldman says moratoriums could touch 45% of planned U.S. capacity, much of it in Texas. Financing hasn't collapsed, though: Goldman counts $67 billion in AI bond deals since October 29 and forecasts $440 billion in hyperscaler debt issuance next year.

stories.headline: Big Tech has $4.49 trillion in AI commitments sitting in footnotes, not on balance sheets
stories.why_read: The off-balance-sheet number is about six times their visible debt. It's the context for every capex and credit headline this week.
body: Alphabet, Meta, Anthropic, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, and Nvidia have disclosed off-balance-sheet obligations for leases, equipment, and power deals that haven't started yet, totaling $4.49 trillion. Alphabet leads at $1.08 trillion, followed by Anthropic at $865 billion and Meta at $810 billion.
Together that dwarfs the $758 billion of debt they carry on the books. Analysts see a windfall for suppliers but warn of real risk if AI returns don't keep pace with spending locked in years ahead.

stories.headline: CoreWeave signs a multi-year deal to train Wayve's self-driving models on Nvidia Blackwell
stories.why_read: A robotaxi rival to Tesla is renting neocloud compute rather than building its own. It's a useful contrast with Tesla's in-house approach.
body: CoreWeave announced a multi-year agreement on November 9 with UK startup Wayve to train its AI Driver foundation models for personal vehicles and robotaxis on CoreWeave Cloud and Blackwell GPUs. It expands Wayve's use of Weights & Biases, which CoreWeave acquired, into full-scale training, evaluation, and simulation.
Wayve says its driver learns from real-world drives across 70 countries. CoreWeave shares rose 5 to 6% on the news ahead of its Q3 earnings, a bright spot against the credit worries above.

stories.headline: Skild AI open-sources Steel, a GPU physics solver that pushes robot simulation to 3.9 million steps a second
stories.why_read: Simulation speed is the bottleneck for teaching robots contact-heavy work. An open solver inside Newton is a real gift to the community.
body: Steel was built with Nvidia and integrated into the open-source Newton Physics Engine. Skild says it delivers up to 13 times the throughput of PhysX on mixed manipulation tasks while using less GPU memory, reaching 3.9 million steps per second.
CEO Deepak Pathak said it pairs with AI-generated environments to speed training for jobs like cable handling. Developers can try it in the browser and contribute on GitHub.

stories.headline: Infineon makes working power devices on the first 300-millimeter silicon carbide wafers
stories.why_read: Silicon carbide sits in EV inverters, solar, and AI data center power supplies. Bigger wafers on existing silicon tools is how it gets cheaper.
body: Infineon says its fab in Villach, Austria, has processed 300-millimeter SiC wafers into functional power devices, which it calls an industry first in a full-scale fab. It did so using existing silicon manufacturing equipment.

The company frames it as securing long-term SiC supply for automotive, renewable energy, industrial, and AI data center customers, and is showing the first processed wafer at electronica in Munich starting November 10.

stories.headline: Fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall 0.4% in 2026, driven by solar, wind, and an oil shock
stories.why_read: A decline at all is news, but the report is clear it isn't durable yet. The 1.5C budget is now under four years of current emissions.
body: The Global Carbon Project's 2026 budget projects 38.2 billion tonnes of fossil CO2 this year, down 0.4%. Oil emissions are expected to drop 1.9%, likely a short-term response to the energy shock from the Iran conflict, and two thirds of rising energy demand is being met by solar, wind, and EVs.
With land-use emissions up slightly, total CO2 is still projected at 43.3 billion tonnes, up from 42.8 billion last year. The remaining budget for 1.5C is about 150 billion tonnes.

stories.headline: Memphis says the SpaceX data center's taxes more than doubled to $54 million
stories.why_read: From today's bookmarks. It's the hard number in the local debate over whether giant AI data centers are worth it.
body: Asked about Elon Musk's claim that data centers have Memphis booming, Mayor Paul Young said the project generated about $54 million in taxes this year, up from about $25 million last year, when it was already Shelby County's second-largest taxpaying property.

Young said the city wants to talk about it in a balanced way, pairing the revenue with protections on environment, noise, traffic, and quality of life, which is the focus of his ninety-day executive order.

stories.headline: SpaceX plans a $24 billion AI supercomputer and its own power plant at Starbase
stories.why_read: SpaceX is building compute and generation side by side so it doesn't have to wait on the Texas grid. That pattern, bring your own power, is quickly becoming the default for AI campuses.
body: The project covers 444 acres near Brownsville, with up to 35 gas turbines providing 748 megawatts for the supercomputer. SpaceX would own and run both the computer and the plant, construction is already underway, and a public hearing on tax incentives is set for December 9.

It lands the same week SpaceX pitched its much larger Arizona campus, and the same weekend Anthropic's gas-generator purchase made headlines. Supporters see a clever end run around interconnection queues tied directly to Starship operations; critics will be at that December hearing asking about emissions and the incentives.

stories.headline: Starship Flight 15 is set for November 13 with a try at catching both booster and ship
stories.why_read: If both catches work, SpaceX recovers an entire orbital rocket for the first time. That's the moment rapid reuse stops being a slide and starts being a schedule.
body: SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT on Thursday, November 13 from Starbase. The plan is a Super Heavy catch a little over six minutes after liftoff, then a ship catch at the tower after roughly 22 hours and about 14 orbits at around 275 km. Along the way the ship deploys 26 Starlink V3 satellites, three of them carrying cameras aimed at the heat shield.

The vehicle flies with upgraded tiles and flaps, and the upper-stage catch only goes ahead after strict safety checks on the way down. Elon Musk calls it a critical step toward rapid reuse, and for a Texan watching from Austin it's a short drive from being a spectator sport.

stories.headline: Canada launches Real-Time Rail, a 24/7 instant payment system
stories.why_read: National payment rails are some of the hardest systems projects around. This one went live with data-rich messaging built in.
body: Payments Canada announced on November 9 that the Real-Time Rail is live. Participating banks, credit unions, and payment providers can exchange, clear, and settle payments in real time, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
It promises instant settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility, and data-rich messages through existing banking channels. HN readers are comparing it with FedNow and other instant-payment systems.

stories.headline: USPS now publishes official ZIP Code boundary polygons
stories.why_read: ZIP Codes are delivery routes, not areas, so every map you've used was an approximation. Now there's ground truth, with quarterly updates.
body: USPS has launched ZIP Code Boundaries, a national map built from its own delivery address and location data. It's offered in internal, enterprise, and publication tiers, each with four quarterly updates.
USPS pitches it to mapping, logistics, insurance, real estate, and navigation users as the ground truth for correcting their existing ZIP data.

stories.headline: Alphabet's Wing plans a $125 million drone factory push, including a plant in Fort Worth
stories.why_read: From your bookmarks. Drone delivery hardware being built in Texas is a nice near-home signal.
body: Wing plans to invest up to $125 million over the next two years in U.S. drone manufacturing, including a new 15,000-square-foot factory in Fort Worth, Texas.

stories.headline: Your TV signal can see through walls
stories.why_read: A lovely physics demo: one software-defined radio and a broadcast TV signal are enough to detect someone walking in the next room and estimate their speed.
body: Recording an ATSC TV signal with an Ettus USRP, the author shows selective fading, where a strong reflection cancels the direct signal. That state turns out to be extremely sensitive to nearby movement: walking around a neighboring room paints stripes on the waterfall.

Each stripe is one wavelength of path change, so from a 70-pixel gap at 150 updates a second he works out a walking speed of about 1.3 meters per second. Any wideband signal like WiFi or LTE works much the same way.

stories.headline: Simon Willison builds a beep triangulator with Claude Code and finds a dying CO detector
stories.why_read: A small, funny, very relatable use of AI coding: five spare devices, a 2007 acoustics paper, and a box room finally explained.
body: Something in Simon Willison's unpacked box room kept beeping, so he had Claude Code build Beep Locator. A Python server shows the map, and phones, iPads, and laptops join by QR code as listeners; they ping each other to estimate positions, with a manual 'rough mode' when that wasn't good enough, and a clap mode for testing.

It located the beep to within about 40 centimeters. Under that pile of boxes was an old carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted new batteries. Claude also dug up the 2007 BeepBeep paper on acoustic ranging with off-the-shelf devices.
